column4: The source section calls sustenance a share and names the fixed portion of inheritance; this verse assigns a portion to both men and women from what relatives leave, including little or much, making the legal share explicit.
At the division, relatives, orphans, and the needy who are present are to be given something from it and addressed kindly; this is the section's inheritance meal in a single scene.
The inheritance shares here are measured by kinship and circumstance, concretely showing what it means for a passed estate to be divided among its rightful recipients.
This ayah gives specified portions to spouses and maternal siblings; it develops the source section's claim that inherited property passes in measured shares rather than being swallowed together.
The final inheritance ruling sets out a sibling's portion, another concrete boundary on who receives a share of an estate.
The verse appoints heirs to what parents and close relatives leave and tells people to give each claimant their نصيب; this directly joins inheritance to assigned portions.
Guardians must deliver orphans' property when they mature and must not consume it wastefully or hastily beforehand; this is a precise limit on taking the estate the section says is being eaten up.
ولا تأكلوا أموالهم إلى أموالكم directly forbids adding orphans' property to one's own and consuming it, the very taking that the section's wording about eating inheritance exposes.

This ayah says that those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire in their bellies; it makes literal the section's link between eating the vulnerable's wealth and the fire brought at judgment.

Asked about orphans, the reply is to improve their affairs and treat them as kin, warning that God distinguishes corrupters from reformers; it gives an ethical boundary for managing the property the section says is consumed.
This command forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity, alongside full measure and just weight; it connects protection of a vulnerable share with fair measure.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best way until the orphan reaches maturity, a direct boundary on the section's image of eating another's inheritance.
Do not consume one another's property wrongfully or use it to bribe authorities; its prohibition supplies the legal opposite of the section's image of consuming an estate wholesale.
This ayah forbids consuming one another's wealth unjustly, except by mutual trade; it marks a general boundary against the unjust taking specified in the section's inheritance scene.
The bequest for parents and near relatives at death shows another way a person's property is apportioned to those who follow, alongside the section's treatment of inheritance.
The prohibition on inheriting women against their will and pressuring them to take back part of what was given marks coercive inheritance as the opposite boundary to a rightful share.

The war-gain ruling assigns a fifth to named recipients and distributes the remainder in its legal setting; the source section explicitly gives ق س م the dictionary sense of dividing booty among its owners.

The verse describes pagans assigning portions of crops and livestock to God and their partners, then distorting the allocation; this is a concrete, contrary use of the section's language of apportioned livelihood.
The Qur'an calls the pagans' allocation of daughters to God and sons to themselves an unjust division, giving ق س م a specific contrary boundary to fair shares.

The distribution of captured wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers is expressly intended to keep it from circulating only among the rich; this sharpens the section's concern with who gets a share.
Alms are assigned to named recipients including the poor and needy, showing provision deliberately directed toward people absent from the wealthy table.
Believers' wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived; that stated claim parallels the section's insistence that need is a claim on what others possess.
The righteous are described as having a known right in their wealth, corresponding to the section's account of provision as an allotted share rather than unbounded private ownership.
This ayah names the asker and deprived as the recipients of that known right, specifying the needy whom the section's hoarder ignores.
The relative, poor person, and traveler are each to be given their due; this is a direct Qur'anic formulation of a portion reaching people beyond its owner.
The relative, needy person, and traveler are each owed a حق; it states the distributive right of the poor in the vocabulary of the section's share and table.
Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, needy people, and travelers; it lays out recipients for the surplus that the section shows being swallowed.

God has favored some over others in provision, yet the favored do not share it with those under their authority; this exposes the social refusal to redistribute the unequal shares the section describes.
Men and women each have a نصيب from what they earn, and the verse directs people to ask God for bounty; this connects the section's defined share to livelihood gained by different people.
نحن قسمنا بينهم معيشتهم states that God apportioned people's livelihood among them; this is the section's central claim about who divides provision.
Allah expands provision for whom He wills and measures it down; this directly illustrates the section's link between رزق and measured allotment.
The same expansion and restriction of provision is attributed to the Lord who sees His servants; it shows that an individual's wealth is measured rather than proof of honor or humiliation.
Allah expands and measures provision for His servants; in its context of created dependence, this repeats the section's claim that livelihood is allotted by God.
The ayah asks whether people see God expanding provision for some and measuring it down for others, identifying these opposite conditions as signs rather than social verdicts.
The formula that God expands and restricts provision appears against claims about wealth and children; the next ayah states that wealth and children do not themselves bring a person near to God.
This asks whether people know God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it down, again denying that a person's share is self-made proof of worth.
The verse says God expands and measures provision while holding the keys of heaven and earth, placing the measured share under divine command.

It explains that unrestricted expansion to all servants would produce transgression, so provision is sent down in a measure; this gives a reason for the section's measured shares without calling poverty humiliation.
After promising provision from unexpected sources and sufficiency for the trusting person, the verse says God has set a measure for everything, echoing the section's q-d-r gloss.
إنا كل شيء خلقناه بقدر gives the section's claim that everything has a measure a direct Qur'anic formulation.
The Creator determines each created thing with precise measure, a direct parallel to the section's statement that everything has an amount and term.
The verse says provision treasures are with God and that He sends things down only in a known measure; it links stored abundance to measured distribution.
Water is sent down in a measured amount and settled in the earth; it concretely joins provision, collected water, and the section's language of measure.
Whatever people spend is replaced by God, the best provider; this reverses the hoarder's belief that keeping a growing stock is what secures provision.

Creatures that do not carry their provision are still provided for by God, while humans are addressed too; this is a specific counterimage to gathering and storing as if stored wealth alone sustains life.
Joseph tells the people to cultivate grain for seven years and leave most of it in its ears; this is measured food storage in preparation for scarcity, unlike swallowing an inheritance all at once.
The seven hard years consume what was stored, except a little kept back; the verse shows a reserve used by measured need rather than amassed for private excess.
The famine plan ends with a year of rain and pressing, the return of abundance after rationing; it completes the passage's contrast between need and provision.
Joseph asks to oversee the land's storehouses as a knowledgeable keeper; controlled reserves serve public need, a specific counterexample to the section's unshared accumulation.
During famine Joseph distributes provisions to his brothers from the storehouses; it stages food allotment to people who have come in need.
Joseph promises to give full measure and calls attention to that practice, an exact scene of food allotted by measure.
Joseph sets a condition on the next measure if his brother is not brought; the boundary shows provision being allocated by a stated rule rather than seized as one mass.
Joseph's brothers describe the harm touching their family and ask for full measure and charity; this is a hungry household asking for its ration and an additional act of giving.
The one who denies judgment is shown shoving the orphan away; this supplies the vulnerable person excluded from the section's table.
ولا يحض على طعام المسكين directly says he does not urge feeding the needy, matching the section's reciprocal failure to encourage feeding.
The person handed the book in his left hand is condemned for not urging طعام المسكين; this gives the same refusal the section cites as a reason for judgment.
Those in the Fire say they were not among those who fed the needy, another explicit account of refusing the food given to the miskin.
The steep ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, matching the section's concrete act of giving food when need is sharp.
The hungry recipient may be a nearby orphan, extending the section's paired concern with inheritance and the meal of the needy.
The other recipient is a poor person in the dust, a concrete image of the weak person whose food the section says is withheld.
They give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite حبّه; the same love that fills the rich person's appetite is emptied into food for people who need it.
Righteousness includes giving wealth, despite love for it, to kin, orphans, and the needy; the section's love of money is reversed into sharing it.

Spending wealth in God's way is compared to a grain that multiplies its yield; the source section's secondary dictionary form حبّ for grain meets its contrast between piled wealth and food given away.
The revived earth produces حبًّا from which people eat; this uses the source section's secondary dictionary form حبّ for grain as actual food, the substance imagined in the needy person's filled jar.
The competition in accumulating more distracts people, a direct Qur'anic occurrence of the source's k-th-r idea of rivalry in wealth and status.
The next ayah says this distraction lasts until the graves are visited; it completes the preceding competition's endpoint and shows wealth cannot extend life.
The one who gathers wealth and counts it is the exact collector named by the section's image of gathering the whole inheritance.
This collector thinks his wealth makes him immortal, the precise false security that the section places beside the overflowing store.
وجمع فأوعى describes gathering and putting away in a container, closely matching both the source section's root لمم for gathering all and its bowl image.
The human is described as intense in love of wealth, a direct parallel to the section's حبًّا جمًّا.
The verse lists love of wealth among attachments preferred over God, His Messenger, and striving; it marks the boundary where attachment to possessions outranks duty.
One cannot attain righteousness until spending what one loves; this turns the section's intense love of money into a test of willingness to give.
This ayah names boasting and competition in wealth and children, then compares worldly life to crops that grow, yellow, and become debris; it joins multiplication, provision, and what passes away.
The owner of two gardens boasts that he has more wealth and supporters than his companion, a concrete scene of possession used to rank people.
The same owner doubts the Hour and assumes that if returned to his Lord he will find something better; this reveals the false afterlife confidence attached to his wealth.
The garden owner's wealth and harvest are ruined and he regrets associating partners with his Lord; this completes the neighboring warning that abundance cannot secure what he owns.
The wealthy say they have more wealth and children and therefore will not be punished; it is a direct example of mistaking abundance for divine favor, which the section rejects.
The response says wealth and children do not bring people near to God, while faith and good deeds do; it breaks the link between a large share and honor.
The verse calls wealth and children a trial, matching the section's account of being tested through expanded or restricted provision rather than thereby honored or abased.
The human transgresses when seeing himself as self-sufficient; this describes the stance that permits the section's wealthy person to ignore the needy.
The following ayah says the self-sufficient one crosses bounds, completing the preceding trigger of imagined independence from provision.
Wealth and children are the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds remain; this gives the section's accumulated property a clear limit.
Those who withhold God's bounty will have what they withheld around their necks, and the inheritance of heavens and earth belongs to God; this directly joins hoarded wealth to its eventual return.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the wealth is held in trust, which reverses the section's claim of absolute possession.
The inheritance of the heavens and earth belongs to God, and the verse urges spending before that return; this directly links present wealth to the source section's final-owner claim.
The verse says God will inherit the earth and all upon it and that people will be returned to Him; it names the eventual return of property and owners in the source section.
The left-handed person asks what his wealth has availed him; this answers the source section's image of love and accumulation with wealth's failure at judgment.
Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings avail him nothing; this is a direct limit on the security the source section's hoarder expects from possessions.
This condemns religious authorities who consume people's wealth wrongfully and hoard gold and silver without spending it; it is a close parallel to consuming inheritance while refusing the poor.
The next ayah shows that hoarded gold and silver heated and used to brand their owners; it completes the warning about stored wealth in 9:34.
The Fire calls the one who turned away, before the next ayah identifies the one who gathered and stored; this completes the section's movement from hoarding the vulnerable's share to judgment.
When good reaches a person, this ayah says he becomes withholding; it names the response to abundance that the section condemns in the wealthy who will not feed the needy.
Immediately after the collector who thinks wealth makes him immortal, this ayah says he will be thrown into the Crusher; it completes the source section's link between accumulated wealth and fire.
This asks about the denier of judgment; the linked 107:2–3 specifies the orphan-shoving and failure to urge feeding that the section treats as that person's portrait.
This ayah says the left-handed person did not believe in God the Great; the following 69:34 separately names the failure to urge feeding the needy, so the moral and social claims stay distinct.
Poor people are described as restrained from traveling and not importuning others, though their need can be recognized; it adds the hidden, self-contained need behind the section's vulnerable guest.
Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, receive their reward; this neighboring statement offers the inverse social practice to the section's failure to encourage feeding.

After the meal in hunger, this ayah describes believers urging one another to patience and compassion; it completes the communal mutual-encouragement dimension without claiming it repeats the food command.

Abraham says he settled part of his descendants in an uncultivated valley and asks God to provide fruit for them; this concretely links the source section's derived س ك ن sense of the needy person's settledness to sustenance that lets a community remain.

The boat belongs to miskin people working at sea, and al-Khidr damages it to keep a king who seizes every sound boat from taking it; this reverses the section's powerful taking the vulnerable's property.
Accumulated gold, silver, animals, and crops are named among worldly desires; this gives concrete contents to the section's object of intense attachment to wealth.
Qarun is told to seek the next life with what God gave him, do good, and not corrupt the land; it shows how large provision can be directed away from hoarding.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but keep a course between; it supplies a boundary to the section's brim-full appetite for wealth.
The hand is not to be chained to the neck or extended completely, lest a person end up blamed and destitute; it contrasts withholding with measured giving.
This condemns miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God's bounty; it names the community-wide refusal to share that the section distinguishes from a lone miser's act.
If people possessed the treasuries of their Lord's mercy they would still withhold for fear of spending; it directly exposes the impulse to keep a stock rather than feed others.
The one who gives and is mindful of God is promised ease; it is a specific opposite to the section's refusal to direct wealth toward the needy.
The next ayah says God will facilitate the giver's ease, linking giving to a provision that does not need to be secured by hoarding.
The person who is miserly, self-sufficient, and denies the best promise forms the explicit opposite of the giver in the preceding passage and matches the section's rich refusal.
The miser's wealth will not avail him when he falls; it completes the section's warning that accumulated possessions do not protect at judgment.
Satan threatens poverty and commands miserliness, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this identifies the fear of scarcity that can keep the section's needy person unfed.
The cups in the Garden are set to a precise measure, قَدَّرُوهَا تَقْدِيرًا; this is a measured cup in contrast to the section's imagined vessel filled to excess.
Hell is asked whether it is full and answers that it wants more; its unfillable appetite is the boundary opposite the source section's vessel filled to its brim.

This ayah identifies the people who counsel patience and compassion after the feeding and mutual exhortation in 90:14–17 as companions of the right; it completes the social outcome while its own contribution is that classification.

Those who spend and do not follow their giving with reminders or injury receive their reward; this adds the section's distinct requirement that sharing the needy person's portion preserve their dignity.
A good word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt; alongside the section's call to speak kindly at a distribution, this marks the boundary between helping and humiliating.
This warns that reminders and injury can nullify charity, giving a specific contrary case to the section's meal and its instruction to treat recipients kindly.
The command is to spend good things from earnings and produce, not what the giver would only accept with closed eyes; it specifies the quality of the share offered to the needy.
The verse says giving charity openly is good and concealing it for the poor is better; it develops the concrete act of transferring wealth to people in need.
The righteous spend in both ease and hardship; this is a specific response to the section's measured changes in provision and its question of whether the needy are fed when others have plenty.
After naming gardens, crops, and fruit as provision, the verse commands giving their due on harvest day and forbids excess; it directly joins food, a rightful share, and restraint.
This says that all things are with God according to a measure, in a passage about what wombs carry and release; it extends the section's q-d-r claim beyond a person's visible portion of wealth.
When prosperity comes, the person says it was obtained through his own knowledge, but the verse says it is a test; this directly challenges treating an expanded share as self-earned honor.
Everything on earth perishes, matching the section's claim that all besides God passes away and possessions do not remain with their present owners.
The next ayah says the face of the Lord remains; it supplies the enduring side of the source section's contrast between what vanishes and the true owner.
Everything perishes except God, to whom judgment and return belong; this is another direct formulation of the inheritance passage's claim that possessions return to their enduring owner.
Qarun's immense treasure is described as so abundant that its keys burden a strong group; this gives a concrete scene for wealth gathered beyond an ordinary share.

Qarun claims that his wealth came from knowledge he possessed; the answer that earlier generations stronger in power and wealth were destroyed confronts the section's mistaken reading of abundance as honor.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, so neither accumulated wealth nor status protects him; this makes tangible the source section's claim that ownership returns and worldly holders disappear.

A treasure is preserved for two orphans until they mature because their father was righteous; this reverses consuming an orphan's inheritance by showing property protected for its rightful young owners.

The ruling invokes orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld and calls for justice toward orphan children; it makes the section's concern with the orphan's rightful portion specific to those denied it within family arrangements.

This ayah warns the measure-cheaters; 83:2–3 specify that they take full measure for themselves and give others less, completing the row's own warning with a concrete parallel to swallowing another's share.
Those who measure for themselves take the full amount, the self-favoring half of a trading-scale case that illuminates the section's undivided taking of an estate.
When measuring or weighing for others, they give less; although this is trade rather than inheritance, it is a precise reversal of fair shares and echoes taking the whole inheritance.
The command is to give full measure and weigh with a straight balance; it supplies a concrete rule for respecting another person's measured due.
In Shuayb's address, people are told to give full measure and weight and not deprive others of their goods; it is a specific boundary against taking the portion owed to someone else.
Shuayb again commands full measure and weight and forbids reducing people's due, repeating the measured-fairness boundary that illuminates the section's swallowed inheritance.
This commands full measure and forbids diminishing what is due, a specific rule for not reducing another person's portion.
The following ayah commands weighing by a straight balance, completing the concrete measure of what people receive.
The next ayah forbids depriving people of their things and spreading corruption; it names the injustice that the fair measure in the preceding ayat prevents.

After describing the person who transgresses upon feeling self-sufficient, this ayah says the return is to his Lord; it completes the section's link between imagined independence through wealth and final return.
